title: West Franks
capsule: West Francia emerged as a distinct realm from the Treaty of Verdun (843), which divided Charlemagne's empire among his three grandsons, assigning the western Frankish territories (roughly modern France) to Charles the Bald. The Carolingian kings of West Francia faced relentless Viking incursions — Paris was besieged in 845 and again in 885–886 — and progressively ceded power to regional magnates; in 911 Charles the Simple ceded Normandy to the Viking leader Rollo. The death of Louis V in 987 without heirs ended the Carolingian line; the assembled Frankish magnates elected Hugh Capet as king, and the Capetian dynasty that succeeded gave the realm its durable institutional identity as France. Our dataset's attestation window ends c. 989, corresponding to the dynastic transition.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The territorial extent of West Francia is broadly known from Carolingian diplomas, ecclesiastical records, and the Treaty of Verdun; internal sub-infeudation means that effective royal control contracted substantially after 850, and maps showing the late Carolingian west represent nominal rather than administrative sovereignty over peripheral regions.
